title: An incremental variant of COEP

labels.name: topic: cross-origin-embedder-policy
labels.description: Issues and ideas around the new "require CORP for subresource requests and frames and etc" proposal

body:
Currently, COEP is enforced recursively across a frame tree. (See [step 6 here](https://mikewest.github.io/corpp/#integration-html).) This makes sense for enabling `SharedArrayBuffer`; without recursive COEP, a frame could be introduced which is not covered by COEP and thus can get its contents extracted. In general, it makes sense for any process-spanning API (like `SharedArrayBuffer`) to enforce that the entire process only contains CORP-opted-in content.

We've run into another class of API where this makes less sense: APIs which do not operate on the whole-process, but still benefit from having specific realms attest that they only contain CORP-opted-in content. A specific example is the [JavaScript agent memory API](https://github.com/ulan/javascript-agent-memory) proposal. The implementer can choose which realms in the agent to return from this API. For security, the implementer must only return realms which contain CORP-opted-in-content. But for this API, it is not necessary to impose the constraint on the whole process, or even on the spec-level agent cluster.

In the same vein, at Google, we've heard from some large sites that they will have difficulty deploying COEP and CORP across all of their recursive dependencies. They are interested in a mode which allows them to incrementally introduce COEP/CORP from the top down, and get some of the benefits (such as security, or access to memory measurement APIs), during a transition period.

So we propose introducing an incremental variant of COEP, which does not need to be applied recursively, and which does not require CORP on iframes. More precisely, the recursion would stop at agent cluster boundaries, which combined with @annevk's latest spec edits that COEP+COOP makes agent clusters origin-keyed, gives us the desired properties. In spec terms, this would consist of:

* A new value (or parameter?) for the COEP header, e.g. `COEP: require-corp-incremental` or `COEP: require-corp;incremental`. This should still trigger the origin-keyed agent clusters when combined with COOP.

* Changing the [COEP matches its parent](https://mikewest.github.io/corpp/#process-navigation-response) check when processing navigation responses to, when the parent's value is require-corp-non-recursive and the child would be put in a separate agent cluster, allow responses with no COEP.

* Changing the [CORP-matches-COEP check](https://mikewest.github.io/corpp/#abstract-opdef-cross-origin-resource-policy-check) when response's mode is "`navigate`" and the result would be put into a separate agent cluster, to no longer require CORP when parent's COEP is `require-corp-incremental`.

* Ensuring that the "cross-origin isolated" bit that SharedArrayBuffer keys off of only works with `require-corp`, not with `require-corp-incremental`, so that SharedArrayBuffer is not sharable for pages that use `require-corp-incremental`.

Note that this does not weaken the guarantees provided by `require-corp` in any way. That is, if the top-level page uses `COEP: require-corp`, then we still can be guaranteed that every subresource that ever loads, including indirectly via child iframes, will be fully CORP-opted-in.

#### Example scenario

Consider `https://example.com/` which embeds `https://widget.example.com/`. `https://widget.example.com/` is not up to date on the latest security best practices, and does not send COEP or CORP. We thus cannot give `SharedArrayBuffer` to `https://example.com/`, since it could use it to attack `https://widget.example.com/`. But `https://example.com/` would still like to set COEP, and it can get all its non-iframe subresources to send CORP.

Without this proposal, `https://example.com/` sets `COEP: require-corp`, and is not able to load `https://widget.example.com/`. (The widget would fail both the CORP-matches-COEP check and the COEP-matches-parent check.) This means the user would see a broken widget embedded in the page. In this world, since the whole process is protected, `https://example.com/` would be able to measure its own memory and use `SharedArrayBuffer`.

With this proposal, `https://example.com/` sets `COEP: require-corp-incremental`. Assuming that `https://example.com/` also sets COOP, this allows `https://widget.example.com/` to load. Now, all of the resources in the `https://example.com/`'s realm are CORP-opted-in, even though those in `https://widget.example.com/`'s realm are not. With this setup, `https://example.com/` would be able to use `performance.measureMemory()` to measure its own memory, but it would not receive memory measurements for `https://widget.example.com/`, since its contents have not been CORP-opted-in. (Neither realm would be able to post `SharedArrayBuffer`.)

Eventually, Example Corp completes its transition period, and is able to get their widget developers to fully enforce CORP on all of the widget's subresources, and put COEP: require-corp on `https://widget.example.com/`. Then, the `performance.measureMemory()` API starts including measurements from the `https://widget.example.com/` realm as well, since now both realms contain only CORP-opted-in content.

At this point, `https://example.com/`'s developers would switch to `COEP: require-corp`. This would help them prevent the introduction of any new COEP/CORP-less iframes, locking in their current security status. It would also allow them to post `SharedArrayBuffer`s.

Thoughts welcome! @whatwg/cross-origin-isolation
